newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cathay stresses ban on endangered species cargo.
newsitem.headline: Cathay stresses ban on endangered species cargo.

text.p: Cathay Pacific Airways is stepping up efforts to ensure parts of animals on the endangered species list, such as increasingly rare tigers, are never flown by the airline, its cargo marketing and sales manager, Ray Jewell, said.
Cathay's home market of Asia is a leading buyer of animal parts which are sold in traditional medicine shops for their alleged aphrodisiac or healing powers.
The Hong Kong carrier said it has begun helping to produce a CD-Rom and manual so airline staff can make a small contribution to help stamp out the trade, which many find abhorrent.
The initiative comes from the airline's environment office, whose staff of three oversees all Cathay's practices to ensure the airline is as environmentally friendly as possible.

Along with Cathay Cargo, the office is working with the World Wide Fund for Nature to develop a user-friendly database of protected species to educate and alert staff on what to look out for on cargo manifests.
"We haven't been flying endangered species because we follow the IATA and CITES conventions on the transport of animals and rare species strictly," said Jewell.

"What we are looking at now is developing a more user friendly method for our counter staff who accept cargo to identify animals and parts of animals and reject carriage if necessary. We are at the initial stage at the moment and can't say when we we will be able to introduce the new system, but it is something we are already quite proud of," he added.
Cathay's marketing department is also being enlisted to produce in-flight magazine articles and seat-back video films to educate passengers on environmental issues.
"Nobody is expecting us to save the South American rainforests or singlehandedly protect the panda, but we can play our part," an airline spokesman said.
